title: Dark energy mystery could be solved by physics we already know
excerpt: The mysterious force pushing our universe apart could be driven by the same subatomic physics that holds atoms together, according to a new study aiming to solve one of the cosmos biggest puzzles.
content:
The mysterious force pushing our universe apart could be driven by the same subatomic physics that holds atoms together, according to a new study aiming to solve one of the cosmos biggest puzzles.

Ever since astronomers discovered that the expansion of the universe is speeding up rather than slowing down, explaining  the cause is one the biggest questions of modern physicists. The unseen driver behind this cosmic acceleration is known as dark energy. Standard cosmological theories usually assume the existence of dark energy requires inventing completely new, undiscovered particles or hypothetical forces of nature.

In a new study published in the Astrophysical Journal, building on the preliminary work by one of the co-authors, Ariel Zhitnitsky, and led by researchers at the University of Sheffield and the University of British Columbia, theoretical physicists have uncovered evidence suggesting that dark energy might instead come from a process called  Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD). QCD is the established theory describing the strong nuclear force that binds fundamental particles called quarks inside protons and neutrons.

Empty space is never truly empty; it is a complex environment packed with subatomic fields and quantum activity. In QCD, this quantum vacuum has topological properties, which can affect space over vast distances. The concept, initially proposed by one of the co-authors, Ariel Zhitnitsky, suggests that as the universe expands, this subatomic structure responds slightly differently over time. This generates an energy shift just strong enough to drive cosmic acceleration without needing any new fundamental particles. The team at the University of Sheffield  helped to compare this model to the latest cosmological data.

“The idea that the quantum vacuum as described by QCD could have the right properties to account for the accelerated expansion of the universe is very intriguing. It raises the possibility that dark energy could be connected to the established theory of the strong nuclear force, without introducing new fundamental fields. Testing models based on this idea against cosmological data is an essential step. Our analysis shows that such a model can reproduce the evolving dark energy behaviour suggested by current observations. This motivates further theoretical work to better understand how the QCD vacuum responds to cosmic expansion and to develop predictions that can be tested with future observations.” Dong Ha Lee, PhD researcher and lead author

When tested against real astronomical data including light from distant exploding stars (supernovae) and leftover radiation from the early universe, the team found that the model matched observations just as well as standard cosmological theories.

“The most striking result is that the observed dark-energy scale emerges naturally from known physical constants, without the need for any additional fitting parameters.”  UBC Professor Ludovic Van Waerbeke

Building on these findings, the team plans to refine their calculations and test the framework against incoming data from next-generation space telescopes, which are set to provide unprecedented detail on the history of the universe over the coming years.
